ADULT EVENING CLASS

Honourable Principal, teachers and dear friends,

I speak today on a subject many people believe is impossible. They say only the young can learn. But a grandmother in our own area is sixty-two years old. She never went to school and could not read. answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Honourable Principal, teachers and dear friends,

A craft can never be learnt only from books. In our village a girl was drawn to pot making from the time she was old enough to go to the fields with her mother. She watched expert potters mix the clay with water, pound it, and rotate the lump with one hand while tapping it with a spatula, and she dreamed of doing the same. But when her mother at last began to teach her, the girl could not even hold the lump of dough, and almost a year passed without her learning anything. What changed her was the kind widow in the dormitory, who told her not to worry and asked her to watch her mother shape the mouth of a pot. My friends, sit beside a skilled person and learn by watching. That is how a craft lives on.

Thank you.

Rhea's grandfather is fond of saying that atoms are only a guess made by scientists. Rhea's teacher disagrees. She explains that a law describes a regular pattern observed in nature, while a theory goes a step further and gives an explanation of why such patterns occur. As examples she names the laws of motion, which explain the jerk a passenger feels when a bus stops suddenly, and the atomic theory, which explains how molecules are formed. She adds that such ideas are always open to improvement and often change as new evidence becomes available, and that this openness is what makes science reliable.

(a) How does a theory differ from a law? (b) Rhea's grandfather calls the atomic theory a guess. State why this description is wrong. (c) These ideas often change as new evidence becomes available. Explain why science can still be called reliable although its ideas keep changing.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) A law describes a regular pattern observed in nature; a theory explains why such patterns occur. (b) A theory is not a guess but an explanation based on careful testing and critical examination. (c) Ideas change on the basis of careful testing and new evidence, and this openness is the key feature that makes science reliable.

Nikhil saw dark clouds at noon and told his sister Pooja that it would rain that afternoon because the clouds looked dark. Pooja asked him some questions: what was the condition of the sky the last time it rained, what is the humidity today, was it above 80 per cent the last time it rained, what is today's wind speed and direction, and is the temperature dropping like it did before the recent rains? Nikhil realised he had only looked at the clouds. Weather, Pooja reminded him, depends on many changing factors such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind, so a forecast uses measurements and models, and very tiny differences in conditions can grow over time.

(a) Pooja's questions made Nikhil's prediction scientifically testable. State what her questions asked for that 'the clouds look dark' did not. (b) Weather depends on many changing factors and very tiny differences in conditions can grow over time. Explain why this limits how far ahead any forecast can be trusted.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) They ask for measurable data and past patterns, such as humidity, wind speed and direction, instead of guesswork from the look of clouds. (b) Because tiny differences in conditions can grow over time into something completely different, forecasts are reliable for a few hours or even a few days, but less certain further ahead.

A Class 9 student places a piece of onion peel and some cheek cells in separate beakers of concentrated sugar solution. After some time the cheek cells shrink, but the onion peel cells keep their size and shape, and the membrane inside each plant cell pulls away from the wall. The teacher explains that the covering outside the cell membrane in plant cells is rigid, and that although it is rigid, water and some dissolved minerals can pass through it, which together with the cell membrane helps plant roots absorb water and nutrients from the soil. She asks the class to name what the plant cell wall is mainly made of.

(a) State what the cell wall of a plant cell is primarily made of, and the kind of substance it is. (b) Both the onion peel cells and the cheek cells were placed in concentrated sugar solution, but only the cheek cells shrank. Using the presence or absence of a cell wall, explain this difference.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Cellulose, a carbohydrate formed by many glucose units linked together. (b) Cheek cells are animal cells and have no cell wall, so they lose water and shrink. Onion peel cells also lose water due to osmosis, but their rigid cell wall maintains their shape, so only the inner content shrinks.

A class held an exhibition on how living bodies are put together. One group's chart began at the bottom with a single cell and climbed upwards. At the first step the students wrote that cells of a similar kind doing a similar job come together; at the next step, that more than one type of tissue makes an organ; and at the step above that, that different organs join to make an organ system. A visitor looked at the chart for a long time and asked why a plant cannot be built as one single mass of similar cells. The teacher asked everyone to answer her using the three steps they had drawn.

Name, in order, the levels the chart shows, beginning with cells of a similar kind and ending with organ systems. (ii) Say what the cells at the first level have in common, and what is added at the level just above it. (iii) The visitor objected that the ladder was unnecessary, since a plant could be built as one single mass of similar cells. Using the chart, explain why a plant or an animal is built in levels instead, and name the arrangement.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Tissue, organ, organ system. (ii) Cells of a similar type performing similar function; more than one type of tissue. (iii) Cells of one kind make a tissue, different types of tissues make organs and different organs make organ systems, so the body follows a hierarchy of organisation in which each level takes its own share of the work.

On it he has drawn a car moving along a straight stretch of a highway, a train on a straight track, children taking part in a swimming race and a ball falling vertically from a hand. questions.stem:
Ravi goes out on a highway and watches a car driver closely. He notes that when a vehicle speeds up its average acceleration acts in the direction of its velocity, while when it slows down the acceleration acts in the opposite direction. He also learns that an average acceleration can come from a change in the magnitude of the velocity or from a change in its direction, or from both. On one trip a bus on a long straight highway moving at 36 km/h had its accelerator pressed for 10 s, so its velocity rose to 54 km/h. It then moved at a constant velocity, and the driver finally pressed the brake and the bus stopped in 5 s.

State the direction of the average acceleration of a vehicle when the magnitude of its velocity is increasing, and when it is decreasing. (ii) Ravi says that because the bus travelled on a straight highway without turning, its acceleration must have been zero throughout the journey. Using what Ravi learns about what gives rise to an average acceleration, and what happened to the velocity of the bus, explain why this is not correct.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) When the magnitude of velocity increases the average acceleration is in the direction of velocity; when it decreases it is opposite to it. (ii) An average acceleration comes from a change in the magnitude of velocity. The velocity of the bus rose from 36 km/h to 54 km/h and later fell to zero, so the acceleration was not zero throughout.

questions.stem:
Rhea works in the dispensary of a small clinic. Instead of weighing every solid she mixes, she measures the volume of the liquid, because that is easier for her. A doctor asks her what a bottle labelled 5% glucose solution contains, and she explains that the percentage tells how many grams of the solute are present in 100 millilitres of the solution. Rhea also has to make a pesticide spray for a rice crop: she mixes 1 mL of liquid pesticide with sufficient water to form 100 mL of spray solution. Her friend asks her about the saline drip used in hospitals, which is 0.9 % m/v sodium chloride, or common salt, in water.

Name the method of expressing concentration that suits Rhea's situation of measuring the volume of a liquid instead of weighing it, and give the two symbols by which it is written. (ii) State what the label on the 5% glucose solution bottle tells the doctor about the amount of glucose. (iii) Rhea's friend points out that the perfumes and cosmetics in the shop next door are liquids too, and asks why they are not labelled in the same way as the glucose solution. Using the situations in which the methods are used, explain.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Mass by volume percentage (% m/v or % w/v). (ii) It shows how many grams of the solute are present in 100 millilitres of the solution. (iii) Perfumes, cosmetics and vinegar are made by mixing two miscible liquids, which is the case volume by volume percentage is meant for; a glucose solution in a clinic is a case where measuring the volume of the liquid is easier than weighing it.

example is 5% glucose solution (Fig. 5.4b). It tells us how many grams of the

He then holds the north pole of his magnet close to the north pole of a second magnet, and afterwards close to its south pole. A visitor asks him to write down the direction of each force he has felt, so that his display card can be read by everyone who comes to his stall.

State the direction in which the force of friction acts on the block as Ishan pushes it along the floor. (ii) State what happens when the north pole of Ishan's magnet is brought close to the north pole of the second magnet, and what happens when it is brought close to the south pole. (iii) Ishan says all three trials show the same force, since in each case something pushes or pulls. Using the direction of the force in each trial, explain why his claim is wrong.

questions.stem:
Meera is in the school kitchen. She squeezes a lemon hard between her fingers, and the lemon gives way and changes shape. On the sports field that same afternoon, a batter swings the bat and the ball leaves his hands travelling in a new direction. Meera says both things show the same kind of force at work, because in each case a push from outside has changed what an object is doing. Her friend Anil disagrees and asks her to say exactly what changes in each case.

State what the force applied by Meera's fingers does to the lemon. (ii) State what the force applied by the cricket bat does to the ball's motion. (iii) Meera says the two cases show the same change because a force was applied in both. Using what the force does in each case, explain why her claim is wrong.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) It squeezes the lemon, so the shape of the lemon changes. (ii) It changes the direction of the ball's motion. (iii) The two forces have different effects, one changing the shape of the lemon and the other changing the direction of the ball's motion, so the same change did not occur in both cases.

changes its direction, and a lemon can be squeezed by the force
applied by your fingers (Fig. 6.1).

State the force with which the Earth pulls the hammer down, and the direction in which that force acts. In a cricket match, a fielder takes a fast-moving ball close to his hands and then, just after catching it, slowly pulls his hands backwards along the direction in which the ball was travelling. In a car, a passenger wears a seat belt, and an airbag inflates quickly into a soft cushion when the car stops suddenly after a collision. A student watching both asks why the car maker thought an airbag was needed at all, when the seat belt was already being worn.

State what the airbag does when a vehicle stops abruptly after a collision, and how this reduces the force exerted on the passenger. (ii) The student says the seat belt alone is enough and the airbag is unnecessary. Using what the airbag does to the time over which the passenger is stopped, explain why the student is wrong.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) It inflates quickly into a soft compressible cushion, so the head and chest push into the bag instead of the hard steering wheel or dashboard; the time of the hit increases, and smaller acceleration means a reduced force on the person. (ii) The bag increases the time over which the passenger is stopped, so the acceleration is smaller and the force on the person is reduced.

Aarav reads that in 1808 John Dalton put forward an atomic theory based on the scientific experiments of that time. Dalton proposed that all matter is composed of indivisible particles called atoms, and that these atoms are the fundamental building blocks of matter that cannot be broken down into smaller parts. Aarav learns that this was the first scientific description of how matter is made, and the starting point for the current understanding of atomic structure. He then finds the questions scientists asked next: what are atoms made up of, what would atoms look like if we could see them, and what makes the atoms of one element different from those of another.

Answer these questions:
1. What did Dalton propose all matter is composed of, and what did he call these particles?
2. How did the earlier idea of the atom, held before 1808, differ from Dalton's atomic theory?
3. Aarav says Dalton settled everything about the atom. Use the questions that scientists asked after him to judge whether he is right.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (1) Indivisible particles, which he called atoms. (2) Dalton's theory rested on the scientific experiments of that time, while the earlier idea of the atom was imaginary and not based on experimental observations. (3) Not true — scientists still asked what atoms are made of, what they look like, and how atoms of two elements differ.

questions.topic: Testing Thomson’s model: The gold foil experiment
questions.stem:
Rutherford's atomic model has the electrons revolving around a nucleus, rather like planets orbiting the Sun, so it is called the planetary model. Rutherford found that the nucleus is extremely small, about one lakh times smaller than the atom. His model explained the results of the gold foil experiment better than Thomson's, but it left one big question unanswered: why are atoms stable? A particle moving in a circular path is accelerating, and an accelerating electron should lose energy, spiral inward and fall into the nucleus. If that happened, atoms would collapse and would not exist, yet in reality atoms are stable.

Answer these questions:
1. Why is Rutherford's model of the atom called the planetary model?
2. A student argues that atoms are stable, so the accelerating electron must be losing energy and falling into the nucleus. Why does the model fail to explain this?

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (1) Because the electrons revolve around the nucleus like planets orbiting the Sun. (2) The model cannot explain stability: if the accelerating electron lost energy it would spiral inward and fall into the nucleus, so atoms would collapse, yet in reality atoms are stable and matter around us stays intact.

Neha is filling gas jars for a school display. The technician hands her a jar of hydrogen and a jar of helium and asks her to label them. She is told that a hydrogen molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms, and that one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom join to form a molecule of hydrogen chloride. answerScheme.modelAnswer: (1) The atoms of helium are stable, so they do not join with other atoms and helium is found only as atoms. The force that holds atoms together is called a chemical bond.

A demonstration tube lies on the science laboratory table, closed at one end by a piston and open at the other. A student pushes the piston forward and pulls it back, over and over. When the piston moves forward it pushes the nearby air particles ahead, so the air in a small region close to it becomes denser than the average. When it moves backward, the air in that small region becomes less dense. The student marks a few air particles with dots on the glass and watches. She sees pulses of denser and thinner air travel the length of the tube, but every dot stays where it was.

Answer these questions on the case:
1. As the piston moves to and fro, two regions of air are produced one after another, one of higher density and one of lower density than the average, while every dot the student marked on the glass stays in its own place. Name these two regions and state what the air particles themselves are doing.
2. In a classroom the air is not confined in any tube, and yet a small sound made at one corner is heard at every corner. Explain what form the compressions and rarefactions take as they spread through open air, and why they can reach every corner.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (1) The denser region is a compression and the thinner region is a rarefaction; the particles only oscillate about their mean positions and do not travel with the wave. (2) The vibrating particles collide with the surrounding particles in all directions, so the compressions and rarefactions spread out in all directions as spherical waves and reach every corner.

Wheat has been grown on Nandita's family farm for generations, and her grandfather chose each year's seed stock from the plants with the most desirable characters. When a disease began to damage the crop, Nandita's father removed the stamens from flowers of the crop plant, tied a bagging around them so that the plant's own pollen could not reach them, and carried pollen by hand from a plant that already resisted the disease. This year the farm also grew a new variety whose DNA carries the genetic material of a desired character placed there by scientists, and the plants that grew from it were high yielding and resisted the disease.

(a) Name the plant breeding method Nandita's father used and state why he removed the stamens and tied a bagging around the flowers. (b) Nandita's grandfather chose the seed stock, her father transferred pollen and scientists altered the DNA. Explain how these three approaches each bring a desired character into the crop grown on the farm.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Artificial hybridisation; removing the stamens and bagging the flower prevents self-pollination, so only the transferred pollen fertilises it. (b) Selective breeding works by choosing which plants reproduce, artificial hybridisation by hand-transferring pollen from a chosen plant, and genetic engineering by inserting the desired character into the DNA, so each changes what the next crop inherits.

reproduction.

covering it with a bagging to prevent self-pollination, and manual transfer of the pollens with
desired characters.

Genetic engineering is also applied by inserting the genetic material of desired
characters into the DNA of the selected varieties.

questions.stem:
Arjun lives in the United States near the San Andreas Fault. He has learnt that this fault runs along a line where two tectonic plates meet, but the plates here do not push head-on and they do not drift apart. Instead one plate slides sideways past the other, and this sliding goes on day after day. Buildings along the line have been damaged again and again by shaking, and Arjun’s family keeps an emergency kit ready because the shaking can come at any time.

(a) Name the type of plate boundary along the San Andreas Fault, where one plate slides past the other. (b) State what this type of movement does to the crust. (c) Explain why a boundary of this kind can cause earthquakes without creating or destroying any crust.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) A transform boundary. (b) The plates slide past each other without creating or destroying crust. (c) This type of movement mainly causes earthquakes, such as along the San Andreas Fault in the United States, and because the plates only slide past one another, no crust is formed or destroyed.

The Himalaya has been rising for a very long time because two huge slabs of solid rock kept drifting towards each other and colliding. Slabs of this kind are called tectonic plates, and they move very slowly, only a few centimetres in a year. Not every collision works in the same way: where a plate carrying ocean floor meets a plate carrying a continent, the ocean plate is pushed down beneath the continent, and soon afterwards the ground begins to shake and a volcano may erupt.

(a) Name the type of plate boundary at which two plates move towards each other. (b) State the landform that forms when two continental plates collide. (c) Explain what happens when an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, and name the two natural disasters that follow.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) A convergent boundary. (b) They form fold mountains, such as the Himalaya. (c) The oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate, and this leads to volcanic activity and earthquakes.

The historian wonders whether her dates are as trustworthy as her colleague’s guesses, and she asks a teacher to explain why the two situations are so different. The teacher points out that one kind of evidence carries exact dates and the other does not.

(a) State how precisely events and cultures could be dated before writing was invented. (b) Explain why a written record that mentions the coronation of a ruler and a war makes dating more accurate. On an outline map of the world, locate and label the following:
(a) Mesopotamia, the “land in between” drained by the Euphrates and Tigris rivers in West Asia.
(b) The Euphrates River.
(c) The Nile River, along which the Egyptian civilisation grew.
(d) The Huang He, in the basin in northern China where the Chinese civilisation grew.
(e) The Zagros mountains, whose crescent-shaped foothills are known as the fertile crescent.

(b) The Vedas are the earliest known corpus because the Harappan script is still undeciphered; Vedic literature existed in oral form for several centuries before it was written down. A group of Class 9 students is making a short film on how India was governed in the earliest times, and they keep making the same mistake. One of them says that the earliest groups of people already had a fully formed State with laws and institutions to enforce them. Another says that nobody governed anybody at all. The teacher points out that what the two have to work out is not a single moment but a process: rules and shared norms that maintain order and harmony, and then, much later, organised political systems with rights and duties of rulers and subjects.

(a) State how rules and shared norms come into being, and what they do. (b) List the elements a State includes, and explain the condition in society under which such political systems developed. (c) Only two minutes of film are left; explain why discovering customs and practices alone would not be enough to show that a State existed.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Rules and shared norms evolve over time to maintain order and harmony, binding social groups into a unified whole. (b) A State is an organised political system based on rules and laws, with rights and duties of rulers and subjects and institutions for enforcing law and order. (c) Customs alone prove nothing, since society is primarily regulated by customs and practices rather than formal laws.

evidence: shared norms evolve over time to maintain order and harmony.

political system based on rules and laws. It includes well-defined
rights and duties of rulers and subjects, mechanisms of governance,
and institutions for enforcing law and order.

questions.stem:
On an outline map of India, locate and label the following:
(a) Kannauj, the main capital of the Gurjara–Pratihāras, in modern-day Uttar Pradesh.
(b) Aihole, a Brahmin settlement to which the Chālukyas gave land grants and which developed into a prominent centre of learning.
(c) Badami, a Brahmin settlement to which the Chālukyas gave land grants and which developed into a prominent centre of learning.
(d) Northern India, the northern part of the large region ruled over by the Gurjara–Pratihāras.
(e) The region of southern India, where the early Cholas formed a powerful kingdom and where King Karikala was found.

markingPoints.description: Kannauj — the main capital of the Gurjara–Pratihāras, in modern-day Uttar Pradesh (1)
Aihole — an agrahāram, a Brahmin settlement to which the Chālukyas gave land grants, which developed into a prominent centre of learning (1)
Badami — an agrahāram, a Brahmin settlement to which the Chālukyas gave land grants, which developed into a prominent centre of learning (1)
Northern India — part of the large parts of Northern and Western India ruled over by the Gurjara–Pratihāras (1)
southern India — the region in which the early Cholas formed a powerful kingdom and King Karikala was found (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) Kannauj — the main capital of the Gurjara–Pratihāras, in modern-day Uttar Pradesh.
(b) Aihole — one of the agrahārams, Brahmin settlements to which the Chālukyas gave land grants, which gradually developed into prominent centres of learning.
(c) Badami — one of the agrahārams, Brahmin settlements to which the Chālukyas gave land grants, which gradually developed into prominent centres of learning.
(d) Northern India — large parts of Northern and Western India were ruled over by the Gurjara–Pratihāras.
(e) southern India — the early Cholas were a powerful kingdom of southern India, and the famous King Karikala belonged to it.

questions.stem: Riya's father disagrees with the rent his landlord has charged and the landlord proposes to settle it privately between the two of them. In steps, explain what the rule of law requires in this situation, and say where that requirement is written into the Constitution.

markingPoints.description: The Rule of Law is a fundamental principle of any democratic society (1)
It ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the law (1)
Disputes are settled in a court of law through procedures established by law, not by force or personal influence (1)
No citizen is punished without following the procedure, and all get a fair chance to defend their rights (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — The Rule of Law is a fundamental principle of any democratic society.
Step 2 — It ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the law, and that no one is above the law.

Step 4 — No citizen can be punished without following that procedure, and everyone is given a fair opportunity to defend their rights.
Step 5 — The principle is enshrined in Article 21, and the rights it safeguards are enforceable in courts of law.

Ved is revising the constitutional framework before his annual test. He makes a card for each point he must remember. The first card says that India has a written constitution. The second card says that more than one political party competes for power. The third card says that authority is divided between the union and the states, and it names this Federalism. Two further cards list the Fundamental Rights and the Fundamental Duties that every citizen of India holds. Ved then meets a friend who studies Canada, where Federalism also appears, but where the power that is left over stays with the union government.

Answer the three questions below.
1. Name the type of constitution on Ved's first card.
2. Name the feature on his third card, and say between which two levels of government it divides authority.
3. Ved's friend studies Canada, which also has Federalism. Compare the two countries: what feature do they share, and how does the power that is left over compare between them?

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. A written constitution. (1)
2. Federalism, dividing authority between the union and the states. (2)
3. Both share Federalism. India's list runs to the union, the state and a concurrent list, while Canada records that the power which remains stays with the union government. (2)

Inside that compound one must then select the element which has the maximum number of atoms. She worked through his equation this way, wrote out each step, and called the equation she got at every stage a partly balanced equation. answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The suffix is ‘one’; the final ‘e’ of propane is deleted to leave propan, and adding ‘one’ gives propanone. (ii) Carbon dioxide, with heat and light. Most carbon compounds also release a large amount of heat and light on burning, and these are oxidation reactions, so a compound gives off the same two things.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
A student wonders why the air reaching her lungs is so much cleaner than the dusty air outside. She is told that in human beings air is taken into the body through the nostrils, where fine hairs line the passage and the passage is also lined with mucus. From there the air passes through the throat and into the lungs. Rings of cartilage are present in the throat, and she learns that these ensure that the air-passage does not collapse. The teacher adds that the surface where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged is very fine and delicate, so it is placed within the body, and there must be passages to take air to it.

State the opening through which air is taken into the human body, and name the two things that line this opening and help to filter the air. (ii) Name the material of the rings present in the throat, and state what these rings ensure. (iii) The surface across which oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged is described as very fine and delicate. Explain why this surface is kept inside the body and what two provisions the body therefore needs.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The nostrils; fine hairs and mucus filter the air. (ii) Cartilage; the rings ensure that the air-passage does not collapse. (iii) Because the surface is fine and delicate it is placed within the body to protect it, so passages must take air to that area and a mechanism must move the air in and out of it.

evidence:
air is taken into the body through
the nostrils. The air passing through the nostrils is filtered by
fine hairs that line the passage. The passage is also lined with
mucus which helps in this process.

Rings of cartilage are
present in the throat. These ensure that the air-passage does
not collapse.

In order to protect this surface, it is usually placed
within the body, so there have to be passages that will take air
to this area. In addition, there is a mechanism for moving the air
in and out of this area where the oxygen is absorbed.

the new generation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.topic: Do Organisms Create Exact Copies of Themselves?
questions.stem:
A biology teacher explains to her class why a child does not end up with twice as much DNA as either parent. She says that sexual reproduction combines the DNA of two different individuals, and that if this happened generation after generation, each new generation would carry twice the DNA of the one before and the control of the cellular apparatus by the DNA would be upset. She adds that many multi-cellular organisms get around this by keeping special lineages of cells in specialised organs, and by a cell division that halves both the chromosome number and the DNA. The students ask her to name that division and to say what happens when two such cells unite.

Name the cell division that halves the number of chromosomes and the amount of DNA, and say in what kind of cells this halving is found. (ii) The teacher says each new generation would otherwise carry twice the DNA of the previous one. State what would happen to the control of the cellular apparatus by the DNA. (iii) When two such cells from different individuals unite during sexual reproduction, explain why the number of chromosomes and the DNA content of the new generation stays the same as before.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Meiosis, found in special lineages of cells in specialised organs. (ii) The control of the cellular apparatus by the DNA would be messed up. (iii) Each cell already carries half, so their fusion re-establishes the number of chromosomes and the DNA content in the new generation.

evidence:
One solution that many multi-cellular
organisms have found for the problem mentioned above is to have special
lineages of cells in specialised organs in which only half the number of
chromosomes and half the amount of DNA as compared to the non-
reproductive body cells. This is achieved by a process of cell division
called meiosis.

the previous generation had. This is likely to mess up the control of the
cellular apparatus by the DNA.

Thus, when these germ-cells from two individuals combine
during sexual reproduction to form a new individual, it results in re-
establishment of the number of chromosomes and the DNA content in
the new generation.

questions.stem:
A gardener plants mustard and papaya in the same garden and watches the flowers open. In the mustard flower she finds both stamens and a pistil, while the papaya flower seems to carry only one of the two. She also notices a faint yellowish powder on her fingers after she touches a stamen, and she wants to know which part of the flower it came from and how it reaches the ovules. A student in the class explains that the pollen must first land on a stigma, and that a tube then carries it down through the style to the ovary, where the female germ-cells lie.

Name the type of flower found in the mustard plant and in the papaya plant, and say which reproductive parts each of them contains. (ii) Name the three parts of the pistil in order from the swollen base upwards, and say which of them contains the ovules. (iii) Once the pollen has landed on a suitable stigma, explain how the male germ-cell reaches the ovule, and state what its fusion with the female gamete there produces.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Mustard is bisexual, with both stamens and pistil; papaya is unisexual, with either stamens or pistil. (ii) Ovary, style and stigma; the ovary holds the ovules. (iii) A tube grows out of the pollen grain and travels through the style to the ovary, where the male germ-cell fuses with the female gamete to form a zygote.

evidence:

watermelon) when it contains either stamens
or pistil or bisexual (Hibiscus, mustard)
when it contains both stamens and pistil.

and the terminal part which may be sticky is the stigma. The ovary
contains ovules and each ovule has an egg cell. The male germ-cell
produced by pollen grain fuses with the female gamete present in
the ovule.

female germ-cells which are in the ovary. For this, a tube grows
out of the pollen grain and travels through the style to reach the
ovary.

questions.stem:
After pollen has been carried to the stigma of a flower, a grower tags it and returns a week later. The petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma have all shrivelled and dropped off, but the base of the flower has swollen into something the family can eat, and inside it there are hard little structures each holding a miniature plant. The grower has read that the two germ-cells that met inside the flower came from the parents, one large enough to carry its own food and the other small and motile. She wants to know how those two cells produced what she is now holding.

Name the part of the flower that becomes the edible swelling, and name the hard structures found inside it. (ii) Starting from the fusion of the male germ-cell with the female gamete in the ovule, name the structure formed first and trace the changes that produce the seed and the fruit. (iii) Both germ-cells differ from one another, and the larger one carries stores the other does not. Name both germ-cells and say how these stores help the zygote to develop.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The ovary becomes the fruit; the hard structures inside are seeds. (ii) Fertilisation gives a zygote, which divides to form an embryo in the ovule; the ovule turns into the seed. (iii) The larger germ-cell is the female gamete, whose food-stores give the zygote the energy to develop into an organism with specialised tissues and organs.

evidence:
After fertilisation, the zygote divides several times to form an
embryo within the ovule. The ovule develops a tough coat and is
gradually converted into a seed. The ovary grows rapidly and ripens
to form a fruit.

One germ-cell is large and contains the food-stores while the
other is smaller and likely to be motile. Conventionally, the motile germ-
cell is called the male gamete and the germ-cell containing the stored
food is called the female gamete.

If the zygote is to grow and develop into an organism which has
highly specialised tissues and organs, then it has to have sufficient stores
of energy for doing this.

questions.subject: Science
questions.topic: Do Organisms Create Exact Copies of Themselves?
questions.stem:
A student asks her teacher whether a baby is an exact copy of its parents. The teacher says DNA copying is accurate, and that if it were less accurate many of the copies made would not be able to work with the cellular apparatus and would die. A new variation, she adds, is made in a DNA copy that already carries variations gathered over earlier generations, so two individuals in a population have quite different patterns of accumulated variation, and since these variations sit in living individuals they do no real harm. Combining variations from two individuals therefore gives a novel combination, she says, and that is exactly what sexual reproduction does.

State what would happen to many of the DNA copies produced if the copying mechanism were less accurate, and say where a new variation is made. (ii) Explain why the variations carried by different individuals in a population can be combined safely, and why each new combination of variants is novel.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The copies would not work with the cellular apparatus and would die; a new variation arises in a DNA copy that already carries variations from earlier generations. (ii) All the variations sit in living individuals and so do no real harm; combining the variations of two different individuals creates a novel combination of variants.

evidence:
If the DNA copying mechanisms were to be less accurate, many
of the resultant DNA copies would not be able to work with the cellular
apparatus, and would die.

Each new variation is made in a DNA copy that already
has variations accumulated from previous generations.

Since all of these variations are in living
individuals, it is assured that they do not have any really bad effects.
Combining variations from two or more individuals would thus create
new combinations of variants. Each combination would be novel, since
it would involve two different individuals.

Combining variations from two individuals therefore gives a novel combination, she says, and that is exactly what sexual reproduction does.

This allowed a more careful supervision over the production process, a watch over quality, and the regulation of labour, all of which had been difficult to do when production was in the countryside. After that the iron and steel industry led the way. With the expansion of railways, in England from the 1840s and in the colonies from the 1860s, the demand for iron and steel increased rapidly. By 1873 Britain was exporting iron and steel worth about £ 77 million.

questions.stem: Priya reads that in the city of Porto Alegre in Brazil, local inhabitants take real decisions about their own city through meetings held in every sector, and that about 20,000 people join in this decision making every year. In about 75 words, and in steps, explain how the city combines decentralisation with participative democracy, and state the changes this method has brought about.

The city is divided into sectors or wards, and each sector has a meeting, like that of the gram sabha, in which anyone living in that area can participate
Any citizen can participate in the meetings that discuss issues affecting the entire city, and the budget of the city is discussed in these meetings

Step 4: About 20,000 people take part in this decision making exercise every year. Farhan's country is a federation. Some of its states want much greater freedom in running their own affairs, while others fear that too much freedom will break the country apart. Read the case below and answer the questions that follow. (a) State the two objectives of a federal system that Farhan's situation reflects. (b) They should agree to some rules of power-sharing, and should trust that each would abide by its part of the agreement. (c) An ideal federal system has both aspects, mutual trust and agreement to live together; an agreement that nobody trusts is not kept.

questions.stem:
Rohan's town holds regular elections and has an elected council. Rohan is sure that because the council is chosen by the people, it will fix every local problem on its own: the leaking taps, the unlit streets and the school roof. He tells his friend Meera that she should stop complaining and simply wait for democracy to deliver. Meera agrees that democracy deserves support, and yet she points out that her neighbours are not at all satisfied with democracy in practice, even though they prefer it to rule by a monarch or to military or religious leaders. She says a democracy can only create conditions, and asks Rohan who must then do the rest.

Read the case below and answer the questions that follow. (a) Rohan believes the elected council will fix every local problem on its own. State what a democracy can do by itself, and who has to do the rest. (b) Meera says her neighbours prefer democracy to rule by a monarch or to military or religious leaders, and yet are not satisfied with it. Name the situation she is describing. (c) Rohan says that if the taps are still leaking after the election, democracy has failed. Using what Meera says, explain why this verdict is not justified and what Rohan should do instead.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) It can only create conditions for achieving something; the citizens have to take advantage of them. (b) A dilemma: democracy is good in principle but not so good in practice. (c) A democracy creates conditions only, so unrepaired taps are not proof that democracy has failed; citizens must use those conditions to reach their goals.

questions.stem:
Dev has read that over a hundred countries of the world claim and practise some kind of democratic politics. He lists what they share: formal constitutions, elections, parties and guaranteed rights of citizens. Then he reads that although these features are common to most of them, these democracies are very much different from each other in their social situations, their economic achievements and their cultures, so what is achieved or not achieved under each of them will be very different. Dev concludes that all democracies must therefore have achieved the same things, and that anyone disappointed in the results has simply misunderstood democracy.

Read the case below and answer the questions that follow. (a) Name the features Dev lists as common to countries that claim to practise some kind of democratic politics. (b) Dev concludes that all democracies must have achieved the same things. Use what he reads about social situations, economic achievements and cultures to show why this is wrong. (c) Dev says a disappointed citizen has misunderstood democracy. Examine his claim and state what such a citizen must do.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Formal constitutions, elections, parties and guaranteed rights of citizens. (b) They differ in social situations, economic achievements and cultures, so results differ. (c) Democracy only creates conditions; citizens must take advantage of them to achieve their goals.
